question.text: Mr. Suresh Kumar, a shareholder in 'Lotus MediTech', wishes to dispose of his shares. The Category II AIF 'Vindhya Capital' holds a Right of First Refusal (ROFR). Under a ROFR (as distinct from ROFO):

answer.text: The AIF must first offer a price, then the selling shareholder can seek a better market offer
The selling shareholder may sell freely but must inform the AIF within 30 days post-sale
The AIF automatically acquires the shares at book value without any market-quote process
The selling shareholder must first obtain the best market quote and then offer the shares to the AIF at that matched quote, which the AIF may accept or refuse

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the AIF Managers workbook on exit rights (p. 296), under a Right of First Refusal (ROFR), the selling shareholder must approach the ROFR-holder with the best quote obtained from market participants. The ROFR-holder then has the right to either match that quote and buy the shares, or refuse and allow the selling shareholder to proceed with the third-party buyer at that price. The Trap: Option A describes Right of First Offer (ROFO), where the ROFR-holder offers first, which is the opposite mechanic. Option B invents a 30-day post-sale notification regime that is not part of the source. Option C invents a book-value automatic acquisition mechanism that is not described in the source. Note: The ROFR is distinct from ROFO precisely because the selling shareholder, not the right-holder, sets the price by obtaining the best market quote first, as stated on p. 296.
